summaryBox.title: Quick Section Summary
summaryBox.takeaway: An ecosystem integrates abiotic and biotic components. Stratification represents the vertical structural layering of plant communities adapted to light gradients, from top emergent canopies down to the forest floor.

conceptBreakdown.codeSnippet:
ECOSYSTEM STRUCTURAL MATRIX
                                         │
         ┌───────────────────────────────┴───────────────────────────────┐
         ▼                                                               ▼
  ABIOTIC COMPONENTS                                            BIOTIC COMPONENTS
  ├── Climatic Regime (Light, Temp, Water)                      ├── Producers / Autotrophs (T₁)
  ├── Inorganic Nutrients (N, P, K, Ca)                         ├── Consumers / Heterotrophs (T₂, T₃, T₄)
  └── Organic Matrix (Humus, Carbohydrates)                     └── Decomposers / Saprotrophs
conceptBreakdown.content:
### 1.1 The Ecosystem Concept
- The term **Ecosystem** was coined by **A.G. Tansley in 1935**.
- Defined as a self-sustaining, functional ecological unit where living organisms (biotic community) interact continuously among themselves and with their non-living physical environment (abiotic factors).
- **Four Fundamental Functional Attributes**:
  1. **Productivity** (biomass synthesis).
  2. **Decomposition** (nutrient mineralization).
  3. **Energy Flow** (unidirectional solar dissipation).
  4. **Nutrient Cycling** (biogeochemical replenishment).

### 1.2 Vertical Stratification in Terrestrial Forests
- **Stratification**: The vertical distribution and architectural layering of different plant and animal species occupying distinct vertical tiers in a habitat, determined primarily by light penetration and physical space.

```
                      VERTICAL STRATIFICATION (FOREST)
                      
   CANOPY LAYER   ──► Top Layer: Tall dominant trees (Emerge into direct sunlight)
   UNDERSTORY     ──► Second Layer: Small trees and woody shrubs
   HERB LAYER     ──► Third Layer: Non-woody perennial/annual herbs & ferns
   FOREST FLOOR   ──► Bottom Layer: Grasses, mosses, lichens, & decaying leaf litter
```

- **Ecological Significance**: Minimizes interspecific competition by allowing diverse plant species with differing light-saturation points (heliophytes in canopy vs. sciophytes in herb layer) to coexist efficiently within a single vertical column.

conceptBreakdown.heading: Aquatic Stratification (Zonation)
conceptBreakdown.title: Aquatic Stratification (Zonation)
conceptBreakdown.content: Deep lakes exhibit distinct vertical zonation: (1) Littoral zone (shallow, rooted macrophytes); (2) Limnetic zone (open water euphotic layer dominated by phytoplankton); (3) Profundal zone (dark, aphotic deep water dominated by heterotrophs); (4) Benthic zone (sediment floor with decomposers).

conceptBreakdown.heading: Thermal Stratification in Temperate Lakes
conceptBreakdown.title: Thermal Stratification in Temperate Lakes
conceptBreakdown.content: Summer heating establishes distinct thermal layers: warm upper Epilimnion, steep gradient Thermocline (Metalimnion), and cold bottom Hypolimnion (4°C), resulting in biannual spring and autumn overturns.
